fields.Front: Define circuit switching and list its four defining properties.
fields.Back:
End-to-end resources (link capacity, buffers) are allocated to and reserved for a 'call' between source and destination for its duration.
1) Dedicated resources, no sharing: circuit-like (guaranteed) performance, constant rate, no queueing.
2) A circuit segment is idle if the call is not using it (wasted).
3) Call setup required before data flows; switches keep per-call state.
4) Used in traditional telephone networks.

fields.Front: Compare FDM and TDM as ways to implement a circuit on a link.
fields.Back:
FDM (frequency division multiplexing): the link's optical/electromagnetic frequency range is divided into narrow bands; each call owns one band for the whole call and transmits at that narrow band's max rate, all the time (e.g., 4 kHz phone channels, FM radio).
TDM (time division multiplexing): time is divided into frames, frames into slots; each call gets the same periodic slot(s) and may transmit at the full (wider) band's max rate, but only during its slot.

fields.Front: Numeric: a 1 Mbps link is divided into 4 circuits. What rate does each call get? In general, how is a TDM circuit's rate computed?
fields.Back:
Each call gets 1 Mbps / 4 = 250 kbps, dedicated but capped (even if the other three circuits are idle).
TDM circuit rate = frame rate x bits per slot = link rate / number of slots.

fields.Front: Numeric: send a 640,000-bit file over a circuit-switched path where every link uses TDM with 24 slots at 1.536 Mbps; circuit setup takes 500 ms. Total time?
fields.Back:
One circuit = 1.536 Mbps / 24 = 64 kbps.
Transmission = 640,000 / 64,000 = 10 s.
Total = 10 s + 0.5 s setup = 10.5 s.
Independent of the number of links: a circuit is end-to-end, no store-and-forward per switch (propagation ignored).

fields.Front: Numeric (slide): a 1 Gb/s link; each user needs 100 Mb/s when active and is active 10% of the time. How many users under circuit switching vs packet switching, and where does 0.0004 come from?
fields.Back:
Circuit switching: 100 Mb/s reserved per user always, so 1 Gb/s / 100 Mb/s = 10 users.
Packet switching: admit 35 users; the link is overloaded only if more than 10 are active at once. Active users ~ Binomial(35, 0.1):
P(>10 active) = sum_{k=11..35} C(35,k)(0.1)^k(0.9)^(35-k) ~ 0.0004.
So 35 users are served with essentially no delay 99.96% of the time.
With more than 35 users the binomial tail probability grows, so overloads become common: queues build and delay and loss appear.

fields.Front: Numeric (textbook): 10 users share a 1 Mbps link. One user sends 1,000 packets of 1,000 bits while the other nine are idle. Time under TDM (10 slots) vs packet switching?
fields.Back:
TDM: the user owns 1 slot in 10, so 100 kbps: 1,000,000 bits / 100,000 = 10 s.
Packet switching: the user sends at the full 1 Mbps: 1,000,000 / 1,000,000 = 1 s.
Circuit switching wastes the nine idle circuits.

fields.Front: Compare packet switching and circuit switching on: resource allocation, call setup, sharing, performance guarantee, best-suited traffic, and example network.
fields.Back:
Allocation: on demand per packet vs reserved for the whole call.
Setup: none vs required.
Sharing: statistical multiplexing, idle capacity used by others vs no sharing, idle circuit wasted.
Guarantee: best effort, variable delay, possible loss vs constant rate, no queueing.
Suited to: bursty data (web, email, files) vs constant-rate voice.
Example: Internet vs traditional telephone network.

fields.Front: Why is packet switching 'great for bursty data', and why is it not a 'slam dunk winner'?
fields.Back:
Bursty sources sometimes have data and sometimes none; packet switching shares resources on demand (statistical multiplexing) and is simpler with no call setup, so idle capacity is used by others.
Cost: excessive congestion is possible, causing packet delay and loss from buffer overflow, so protocols for reliable data transfer and congestion control are needed. Open question: how to give circuit-like bandwidth guarantees to audio/video.

fields.Front: Give the human (restaurant) analogy for reserved resources vs on-demand allocation.
fields.Back:
Circuit switching = restaurant that takes reservations: hassle up front, but a guaranteed table.
Packet switching = no reservations: no hassle, but you may have to wait for a table (queueing) or be turned away (loss).

fields.Text: Circuit switching: resources are {{c1::reserved}} for the call giving {{c1::guaranteed (circuit-like)}} performance, but idle circuit capacity is {{c1::wasted (no sharing)}} and {{c1::call setup}} is needed; used in {{c1::traditional telephone networks}}.

FDM: each call gets its own narrow {{c1::frequency band}} all the time. TDM: time is divided into {{c1::frames}} of {{c1::slots}}; each call uses the {{c1::whole band}} but only during its periodic slot.

1 Gb/s link, 100 Mb/s per active user, active 10% of the time: circuit switching supports {{c1::10}} users; packet switching supports {{c1::35}} users with P(more than 10 active) < {{c1::0.0004}}, computed as a {{c1::binomial}} tail probability.

Packet switching suits {{c1::bursty}} data (resource sharing, no call setup) but allows {{c1::congestion}} (delay and loss from buffer overflow), so protocols are needed for {{c1::reliable data transfer}} and {{c1::congestion control}}.
